blocks.x: Why don't you let me ask the question? That's okay. I've already looked into your history a little bit. So you started playing at the Hall, what, probably in the mid-60s?

Well, the Hall had opened up a little bit, but if you had Larry Boyce, he'd open it up for pleasure. And when I came back in 1968 to Chicago, I don't know if that's the exact year. No, no, no, no, no. I'm sure I made a mistake there. It was before that. I had been in Chicago before. But anyhow, I wasn't playing guitar, so I wasn't interested in the music. I played in my younger days. So I used to hang around George Gantt over and go get a profession on my banjo playing, you see? And he used to let me sit in a couple of while, see? And so then they put me with a band. It was a Sweet Dumbas band, Percy. And from there, well, you ask the question from there.
Okay. When did you drop the, well, all right, so you started, when you came back from Chicago in 68, you started at the Hall?
No, no, I came back in 40. That's what I made a mistake of me. Oh. I actually came back in 40.
But didn't you spend a few years, like from 65 to 68, in Chicago again?
I went back the second time. Yeah. For about three years or so.
I worked at Jazz Limited.

I took a fellow named Mike, he was a very versatile man like me. He played guitar in bands and sang, and he was older than me. He was down here when Louis Armstrong came to me on you somewhere in the 30 and played somewhere out there in the middle.
And you were playing banjo at this time?

At that time I was born for the Stikker Steamboat Company. Uh-huh. And there was a ten piece band. It had three sax, three brass, and four rhythms. And you had to play banjo, you had to play pangeline guitar. If you were bass, you had to play bass following and bass horn. I worked with, I started with Fate Marble, and then they had a job with Sidney Desveen, and that's where he came to me. We used to play at the country club on Sundays. And that's where the Captain Vaughan came in and heard the band and I used to put on them, so we got the job with them. Which band? No, Sidney Desveen got the job, I'm sorry, because he was already working. They had another book called, something from Cincinnati down there. And his band should play, he was having trouble with them, so he hired me. I was working on top of the Astoria. Lee Collins, that's when I recorded that thing they called it, Astoria Hot 8. We had Sid Averdino clan, that white man. That's what we call that the old Italian Hall. That's the first recording I ever made. So from there, I went with Sidney and went on the boat there. Sidney got the job on the boat. And then I worked with Sidney, I don't know, one or two years. And then I went with A.J. Peer on. And then, it was Friday, 38, they dropped us off in St. Louis, gave us a train ticket to go back to New Orleans. And I went to the captain I was visiting. I stayed around St. Louis for a while. And I told the captain I'd like to visit New Orleans. So I went to Chicago, I mean. So I went to Chicago, a buddy of mine, he's married, and he had family, and had a room, and so he asked me to stop with him. So I ended up staying up there, 30 years to 40 years.
Yeah, for about ten years. And that's when you.
I was doing all combo work. I wasn't playing no band in there.
That's when you were playing the guitar mainly. Yeah. And I gather you had one of the first amplified guitars in the area.
Well, when I get to all Bart Chubb, I was probably one of the first black to have an electric guitar.
Uh-huh.

Yeah. Well, other fellas came after, they weren't safe that way. But they had a lot of white musicians had an electric guitar. Because I was dealing with the wheel line from way back then, in the late 20s and all through the 30s and things like that, up to today.
When did you start playing the electric guitar? In Chicago or on the uh?

No, I was working in New Orleans. Oh. In New Orleans, yeah. I worked in this band, had electric guitar. Yeah. A couple of other guys got them out to meet. Kimmel Garfunkel and A.J. Monner and a couple of other fellas. George Gainer.
What sort of music were you playing at that, you know, when you were playing there?
Well, at that time I said those were in ten piece bands.
Oh, so you were playing the electric guitar in the ten piece band?

And the band, yeah, yeah. Just about the last, before, the 38, the last two years, the captain told me, you don't need the band, you know, most everybody wants to listen to electric guitar now. So for that two years I didn't play it on the boom. So you were playing the guitar in the boat? Yeah, but I didn't want to listen to the guitar because, you know, well, the band was going out as far as those kinds of bands, you see. Banjo was going out.
And in Chicago what type of music did you do?

Well, I got away from bands. They had a lot of three pieces, four pieces of combo in the yard. And I got with a fellow named Melvin Banks and we got with a fellow named John Creech, Papa John Creech, he played up at the Roses. And we organized a group, we called ourselves the Chocolate Music Balls. And we got jobs through bookings, some jobs came through the union, and we would go on, well, not tour, because we'd be working for a hotel chain, and we'd probably be, which would maybe be four weeks, six weeks, or eight weeks. We'd play most of the time, if it was four weeks or eight weeks, they'd hold us long, long, you see. And we did a lot of those, and I know we played Fort Wayne, we know we played Indianapolis, we went a way up in north of South Dakota, and a lot of other places, I can't mention, mention, mention, all in the northeastern state, from the Orleans, you see. At that time, most places had, they didn't have, besides, most places didn't, too, they have dance ball going on, but they had started with cocktail music, see. It's hotels, or they might be in a certain restaurant, a popular restaurant or something. They may walk me out, one of the places, they played quite a bit. Oh, yeah.
Then I gather, well, like up in Chicago, you know, things started drying up a lot. I mean, it started.

Yeah, things started drying up around about, let's see, around, around, about, in the mid-forties, 45 or 46. Mm-hmm. I stopped playing with the most guys to stop, and I had a second wife there. And I went, I got a job in the lawn, just sorting out clothes, and I got to be what they call a spotter. That's slower Don than a friend of mine used to preach to you. He had a beautiful voice. And, can't think his name right now, he was working at a founder where he made the foam plows, you know. And I was scared when I went in that place there, but I knew I had two friends in the foamer, the black foamer and the white foamer on my side, so they made a barrel grind out of me. That's what foam, this is to put on the foam plow, and you have to soften them on the end, you know. It was hard work, but I stayed there until they started laying off.
But you were playing a little bit of music on his side?

A little bit of them, no, not too much music then. When I worked at that, I didn't play all that, I worked at that founder, I didn't play all the time playing completely. Because there were things that I was actually slowing down, you know, around 46, 47.
Then you came back to New Orleans and you stayed there.

Yeah, and then I, the second while I had, we would be together, then we'd separate, and we'd come back together, and I just, I came out to visit, and my people had bought a place on Corneyes Street, and I came, when I went back, the Dland later died, so I stayed about a week more at the Bell Range, her funeral and everything, and I came back in 48, all the way up until 65, and I went to take Mike's place after Chad Limited. I stayed there three years. And things was awful around, Chicago music, man.
How was it down here when you came back in?
Well things were problems with Preservation Hall, old mufflers, old mufflers, a lot of guys down here. I don't know, I'll say 60, me. Some people say 62. Well the Jaffees took over in 62.
Yeah, well that's when he took it over.
They had Bernstein, and then they had another lady with him, and then another little fellow from California, a cripple, right?
He tried it.

And that's when Jaffees did him, was going up I think at Tulane University, because you see, we used to play for all of them way back there, Tulane University. And then they took it over, and it's been successful ever since. That's probably about like 62, like you said. Then they started having concerts, you see, the first one, Iowa, was in Japan, yeah, in 19... No, I went somewhere because I was with George Lou's band, yeah. We played some old Cincinnati, and then St. Paul, the Twin Cities, and a couple other places, some places in Virginia, you see. So, after George's band, George died, and the band held for a little while, and then went down with... Then they took over the band, you see. And they pushed him when Willie got in there, you see. And I got a record to me, but that was made in the Twin Cities. And I recorded with Punch Miller, and all of them. Punch Miller was pretty good. And so, then they put me in with the... The Kid Thomas band, because they had a concert tour, and Charlie's wife was a piano, but their wife was sick, and he decided that... Bless the world, because I couldn't make it. So they put me in the band, and I didn't know I was going to stay in the band. When I came, we'd come back off the concert tour. I found, they'd say, come in tonight, you know, come in tonight. Next week, come in tonight, same night, so I'd stay here.

Uh-huh. Yeah. And like from, you know, when you came back to New Orleans to about, what was that, 45, I mean, 48 to 65? 48, 48. Yeah. You were, you found, you played quite a bit of music in that time, didn't you?

No, I had to get around and see the fellas. I had to stop playing all the good, you see. I'd get around and see if you look the fellas I knew, went all around the city's fellas I knew. We had a lot of places more than they have now, but blacks even looked up and white. And guys, I started fooling practice management more, and that was all the lecture you get there, you see, because I already had one, you see. And, like I said, in the hall opened up, everybody got interested in that, see. Yeah. But I was, I didn't, I didn't want to go to work right away. I took about two, three months for us to stay awake and see.
But you didn't have, you didn't find it necessary to get a job and a found, you know.

No, no, but I had a family home. My mother's father were living. Uh-huh. And she had a daughter, had a child, and my mother's father took care of it. And my oldest brother, he lived this block and a half from here. And he was, had a, well, he had a woman with the other, well, he had a brother. And I was told my mother, told him, say, you better go down there and stay pregnant with them. You know, the only one, they finally got married, see. Yeah. So that left me and my sister there, and then, and my mother's father. And my mother passed away, I was awful shocked to my father. So at that time I was playing with different people, you know, different people. And I started practicing a whole lot of them, I used to be more, you see. Because I could, at that time, like I said, we'd play in combo, where we played all organic music. We had vocal parts, we had novelty songs, we had, took some of the popular big band songs, played with three pieces because people would act for them, you see. And in that kind of job, in them days, if you didn't make no success enough to draw people for the man to make a profit, you wouldn't stay there long. But we always kept the jump to hate. I used to go buy music and get music with fellas, and we'd have rehearsals and get them down, vocal, instrumental and everything. Yeah.
When you were coming up, you know like when you first started playing banjo, your idol was John Marrero. That's right.

One of them, I always met John Marrero, but John Sincero was living up in Chicago, I think, and I used to copy some of his stuff. And I actually copied some of Les Paul, the other guy who used to be with, Benny Goodman, a black fellow, he died. He's all a Christian. He's a great way. You have to do that to keep yourself voices down, you see.
What did you like about Marrero? I mean you took over, I mean you saw him quite a bit, I gather, down here. What about his playing did you like? I've never saw him.

Well the whole band itself, my daddy was very rich and my daddy were very good friends, and also some other things. I don't know what's happening. John, no, that's how this happened. Well I used to listen to that fellow, young fellow, you'd go to dances and things like that, and listen to that, the fellow's playing. And they had another fellow named Cap of Daringberg who played on the roof garden after John Grabber and we, I still call it, I don't know what they call it, something else, the building is still there. And they had the Pelican Hall, they had a lot of places down in this area, they had a hall, and I used to go down and listen to that Sam Morgan band, see. They were very seldom used as piano. And you admired a fellow that was older than you and played better than you. And another fellow when we had the, when we had the, when we had the Depression, when we had the, I don't know what they called it, in other words, he used to go to rehearsal every day, and you got paid, you know, and I was still in the Depression. With WPA? WPA. Yeah. I didn't join that because I was with this first wife of mine, I was standing on the Harbour and something, and the supper I was working with the city band, and I used to arrange the fellows, and I'd have different little groups and bands and things, and it was in my way. In fact I did better than playing music and writing arrangements and teaching than if I'd went on the WPA because I'd have been confined to go to rehearsal every day, see. So I made that out there. And this Nelson, he was with Sidney Duesley Band at the time, and the guys that were living with, most of the guys were probably dead now, yeah. But I would never thought about playing band, you know. And that E-Haw program, I would have listened to that one in which bar radio, one out from, was that Tennessee, the old opera house, and the E-Haw program. I'd have listened to all that kind of stuff, way back there, my radio, see.
You said you would have never thought about playing banjo?
Yeah, when I was there in Florida and all over the month. Oh, when the Hall was there, yeah.
Yeah.

That's the only reason why I went back on banjo, you see. Yeah. And like I said, I enjoyed Luce Band, and when I came back, like I said before, I lost my scene now after so. So Punch had a Sunday night date there, and he requested for them to hire me. So I stayed with that band. When Punch died, and there was some other trumpet player, and that's why. Then they made it Sweet Emmons night, called it her band, Pussy and Willie Humphrey, came in there and started playing. Now they're the top band today, because Jaffa is the managing leader of that band, you see. So when I went to Chicago, I lost my scene out there. I went to the jazz, and that man called me to Wicker Mountain. And the fellow died. Well I was single, I wasn't married to this woman, and I was single, I had to stay up there. Until the place closed up. The man had me on notice for about two or three months. Every month he had to give me a notice, you know. He couldn't make up his mind. So my wife wouldn't come back. I said, no, we're going to stay here until he's given me, tell me, you've got to give me a four-witch or two-witch notice, you know. And we had a big place up there, man. She had come from California and I got married, honey, I got married up there. I'm my third husband, and she's my third wife.
Yeah. And so you played some at Preservation Hall before you went up to Chicago?
No, at Preservation Hall. And you said 60, I said 60.
Yeah, no, but I mean before you went to Chicago the second time. Oh, the second time, yeah.

Well, that's what I say, I lost my seniority. I went to work at the Red Guard, but I went to work for two nights. And those guys, they really didn't know anything about banjo, you had to play that. But I had, just like I say, coming up in my lifetime, I always learned songs, they come out, most of us just in my age, you see. Mm-hmm.
How did you, you were, how many years in Donaldsonville? Only about seven.
No, I was born in the house of the house. Yeah. Half the band, just children born and all about half born in the audience. Uh-huh.
How old were you when you moved?

Oh, I was almost a young boy. I remember going to kindergarten school, and I remember going to the only public school I had for blacks, out at the end of River Avenue. And when we come to New Orleans, we move on, and Boydhead and Oak, I was going to the, we could call it the, the church on the side of Cowden Avenue, it's still there, but they called it something else. That's where I made my first communion, so I must have been very young. When you first? First communion, because I'm catechic, see, and conforming and everything. They did call it St. Dominic, but they didn't change the name of it, you see. And then we moved into the Garden District, because I went to Holy Ghost School. And then, that's where my daddy, like I said, sent me to the professor, Dave Perkins, to learn music and he decided I should learn violin. But all I got out of him was learn how to read music and everything.
Did you play any banjo before you went to the band?

No, how the banjo came about. My brother was working at the war lines, and he bought a banjo and I was teaching him, and he got discouraged with him, and I bought the banjo back from him. I bought him. And I taught myself the banjo. And the guitar, I taught myself for a reason, because I had already learned music through playing the violin, you see. You could do those things.
So the first instrument you learned was the violin? No, the guitar.
The guitar from your father?
The air training, yeah.
Yes sir.
And then when you went to Dave Perkins, he taught you the violin? The violin, yeah. He didn't play the violin, he just knew.

The one thing about it, I didn't learn to like somebody playing the violin, a teacher, you learn to position the thing out of, you know, to regulate your hands, like you do with any strings. I didn't learn that, but I did learn how it was a pretty good reader on it, you see. I didn't learn how to jazz on it or nothing, you see. You look at yourself.
And your father played the guitar? Yes, he played the guitar.
He played the guitar, the viola, because they had a viola around the house all the time. But naturally after the family got, you know, growing large, he had to stop playing music completely, you see.
Yeah, to support the family.

Yeah, he played with a trio from out there in the Irish Channel. And then he went to a band called the Silver Leaf Band. And the man worked for the old Keith Copper Company, that's the way he flew to the time. We don't see you that for him.
Yeah. And was your father's, you know, when your father tried to teach you, was he really strict about trying to teach you? No, he wasn't strict.

He had had came about, they had to get through there, you know, laying against the wall or something, doing something. My other brothers used to fool with it, and I would fool with it more, because my mom would tell him, you know, we weren't supposed to fool with it, but we'd ask permission. So he took us one day on up to the house on the ramparts, see, 20, 23, they call it Danny and I. And they showed each one of us some chord structure. I think it was three or four days. And he found out that I was the only one that couldn't remember. And that's why he said, you're going to the strangers with Professor Poitgen, who didn't live about, let's see, two and a half blocks or three blocks, three and a half blocks from where we lived. And that's why I just said I was just trying to do it with him. See, they had guys who were playing violins back in those days that I knew.
Yeah. You were playing violins in bands? No, no, no, no. Because a lot of people learned on violins, I find.
The only thing I can say about the violins is to learn how to read music.
Because I think Willie Humphrey. The Willie Humphrey family?

Yeah, Willie. First learned on a violin. His daddy, his daddy was a famous clown to play, made a movie out there in what he called Hollywood today, when they had silent pitches. My father knew the family very well.
But he also learned, I think his first instrument was violin.

It could have been, see that was a song of a style like that. It was either piano or violin in those days. Of course you had the brass instrument, but they wanted to take up the brass instrument, you see. But the same thing that was mostly a must, piano and the violin. For learning.
You either chose one of those two and then branched out.
For you to branch out in music, you see. And these kids today don't realize the opportunity they had that we didn't have. They get all that for free. And good teachers and everything.
You worked your way. Didn't you work for your music lessons?

Yeah, well after I made my first communion I had made an oath that my mother and father would never have to buy me nothing. And I worked after school. I worked like all that area from Jackson, all over to Louisiana Avenue, and on the other side of St. Charles. Them white people, my people knew. All of us did that. My oldest sister, my oldest sister, Dr. Brun, which was one of the most Philippine, that's Philippine Britannia. And I worked on 3rd and Britannia, and I worked at a Hill Drug store right there in Washington,
Britannia.

The man liked me so much, I started there in school. And, no, when school was closed, I told him, we started going back to school. He said, well, you can come in after you come back to school. I worked until about, I closed up 11 or 12 o'clock. And I did yard-boy-wake, port-wake, little way to work and everything. I could go to work and other places on 7 and Coliseum. These are all rich people. My daddy knew it. My sister got jobs and everything. Them brothers got jobs and everything like that, you see. And that's why I said I paid my own music lessons and bought my own clothes and everything. When did you find time to practice? Huh?
When did you find time to practice? Oh, I found time to practice, yeah.

That was a must to me. Nobody had to tell me that, sure. But it must have been hard finding time if you were going to. Well, no, you were young and you were trying to make out you come from a poor family. I say poor, I mean we did have a place to sleep. We had to eat three meals a day and having a whole lot of clothes. Well, no, very few had the whole lot of clothes in those days. You know, you had maybe a suit, you called your son a suit, or you were going out a suit, a suit. Yeah. Then I got a job working for, let's see where the temple lay on it, or St. Charles and Padilla. My daddy was working there. He worked there a long time until he retired. St. Charles and Padilla. They had a cleaning place, a Howard cleaning place, right across from Beepin Shore. It's a spaghetti house now. And I was working there. When school closed, when school closed.
See?

No, I wasn't working there when school was open. I don't think so. And I worked there. I had a place on Canal Street. I think it was a white jewelry store. Then I worked for Whirline, when Boerese, Miss Boerese had it. And after he found out my ability, he really knew Perkins, because Perkins used to come in the Groomwall store and had a Whirline store, which is still there. And I was supposed to run the elevator and help him behind the—keep stocks of all the things like strings and like things for the horns and everything. Then on the next floor, they had a repairman. Now, he was teaching me how to take a horn apart and put it in that asset and thing. And when school time comes, he was saying with me, my daddy demanded I go back to school. So I lost that job, you see. That was a pretty good paying job, you see. And if I knew about an instrument thing, I knew how to clean the violin, the shell over, string it up, put new strings on it and things like that. Wipe it off at the time, knew how to restock up the strings, all the string instruments for the read instruments and everything, you see. And most times in those days, the Whites and some of them Blacks, they couldn't read. I remember this drugstore, on the Hill Drugstore in Washington for times, they had, sometimes, a lot of white fellows couldn't read. They had a good memory. They had a few Whites. The man would get mad about them, tell them in front of us, say, you know, these fellows say, oh, I say, Magnus, he wasn't going to school, so why can't you read?
When did you start playing music professionally for, you know, your first few jobs?

Well I wasn't calling myself a professional before, before 24. I was in ninth grade, 35, right there, F1-0. And these two guys was taking lessons. This man and these guys were married men and everything. They left in the days first. The Trammer played George Morris, and Trump was played Thomas Mack. And the saxophone player, Edmund Washington. I just buried them this year, first part of this year. And they used to get a little job, they used to hire me. They had family and everything. I mean, they were work guys, married and everything. And so we got this job, a fellow named Joe Wynn came to, and he all in looking for a bang. He went up on the roof, Gordon, a couple other places. So he contacted, some way he contacted this guy, the one that worked with, he was sort of a porter at the Groom Hall or something like that, an old hotel. And so we used to get jobs, you know, on the weekends, like maybe Friday, Saturday, Sunday, like that. And so this man came to the, and he decided to take us. His name was Joe Wynn. He was just sort of a gambler and a son of a guy. He wasn't a help of a gentleman. I saw Peter Rayford, he was with us when we were to get jobs, you see. So we told him that when we were going, we couldn't take him, and he didn't like it. So we told him that if anything was possible that we were having trouble with this guy, we sent one. So it was a black organization. These people were very, I've seemed very proud of them, because we had them all down here. They were black masons, and they were in business. You know, they had them own property. A lot of them owned, had their own business. One of the doctors was, the doctor, the black doctor, and he had his own drugstore. This man, Aaron, had his own cab stand, had his own restaurant, and had his own meat shop. And there's this either Aaron Long and the doctor, and somebody else. And they had a park. In those days, most black cities, they had their own amusement park. They'd have their own baseball game, baseball team. That's what these people had in Pensacola. They had it in Mobile, I know. And Montgomery had the same thing. So I was making twenty-four dollars work. My dad was making about, I was working only three days a week. Sometimes they'd double or something, but they'd still pay the twenty-four dollars a whole lot of money. My daddy was making about fifteen to seventeen dollars working at the Pee's and the Temple. And then seven on Sunday, because the elevator man would take off. See? And we made a big hit. On Pensacola. We called it the Pensacola Jazz. See, during those times, there were people who would hire different bands from the Orient, because on account of the people who took a racket to the Orient Jazz Music. Mobile got popular with it. We had a black man named Gomez at Dennis. He opened up a place. They had places before him. You see? And those places did that to make money. They had the ground and everything. They were like a pavilion. I don't know if you know what the pavilion was. They had them out at the lake. They had them in some of the parks and everything where you could play. But these were owned by these people. The organization. And that was my biggest achievement in my success. In life, the song that I was going to be a musician, instead of playing the music. See?
Yeah. So you decided pretty much in Pensacola that, or?

When I was there, we were stationed there, but we did a lot of traveling. Travels, uh-huh. Yeah. We even played for some white people. There was a battle house hotel in Mobile and a hotel in Pensacola on Palafonchia, I think that was the Man Street, and a couple of other places. But I'm just showing you how that music was popular, getting popular way back up in there.
Did you have to play any differently for the people in the country, you know like in Pensacola, than you did? No.

We played our one star, which we all called it. It's what they called tradition, not Dixieland. But we did have reading music, reading musicians, because why we made it better than the other guys, because we could go by the sheet music and learn the songs. In those days when the songs were changing quite a bit, and if the bands didn't learn no songs, the people wouldn't hire them. And if you didn't play the right tempo for them people to dance, the man wouldn't hire you. But we understood all that. And learn how to get along with people and make yourself pleasant with people, you see, make people like you, you see. And they used to do the same thing like I just said in Pensacola Mobile, when you all in there, you had black clubs, organizations around you, and you had to go to Ballyhoo. You had to go advertise on the truck. You used to use a furniture wagon. That's how they called it a tailgate ramble in there, oh they did. Then they went to Automobile, little trucks putting you on. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Then they went to automobiles, little trucks, put in your arms. And they had radio that had come out, but everybody didn't have a radio. They used to use it for, not only the music, new chords would come out. They used to use bands to go down and ballyhoo, let the people know the new chords would be out and everything. See, it was quite a few people to work. And then of course I didn't play in the funeral none of that because I wasn't a brass or a reas. Had a lot of organizations that had already contracted for the people that died, they'd have a funeral with a band with them. You see they had them all in the football city city. How you could do that. And they had a lot of dancing places, small and large and everything. So there was a lot of work, not only in yards and other places, wherever we went, where I went.
When you were advertising, what, if you were playing a dance at night, you would go around in a furniture wagon or in a car and play, a truck, you know, and play throughout the city?

No, you had certain areas you went into. You couldn't call it where the hall was. You would go to approximately, let's see, twelve or twenty-four blocks in the area, or twelve, in that area. Because, I mean like uptown, back of town, or front of town, if it was in that area, you would go around Balli-Hood in that area, you see. And the people liked the way the band sounded when it was Balli-Hood, they'd come to the dance. If they knew the musicians, the people that went to dance, they knew a lot of the musicians, black and white, they knew. They'd come to the dance. And then in your age, you had your time, your season, your elect season, most everything dropped down slowly, you see. But right after Lent, everything's opened up, you see. So, like I said, that was the slowest part of the year, Lent. Well, the British people were Catholic, they'd go to the dance, you see. Yeah, that's a wonderful thing, man. So, like I said, you have to, music is just like any kind of trade or business you have. You're competitors all around. You like to build yourself up to be popular and do things to please the public. And if you, like I said, the band that didn't, people would try them out. And if they didn't have that flow dancing, that man would get another band.
How long did you stay in Pensacola?

Oh, I think it was, let's see, I went there in 24, I must have came around about, no, about 20 years, about three years, about 27 years. I said, well, when the job was closed and we left Pensacola, and one stayed in Mobile, and they had a union there. They had a union in Jacksonville. We didn't have no union, black union in New Orleans. And when I was coming back, I told my daddy, this thing was really getting bad. And I, people always taught me, always had something to say, you know. I wrote and told my daddy, I was staying in Mobile, we wouldn't do any much, because the guys that had a union there was blocking us out, see, because we were staying there, didn't mind us coming through, you see. So, he said, come on home, boy. He said, you got, I got a job for you. And the very reason, his brother had got what the man, one of the people, the man that owned, had something to do with the Forsyth Brewery. He had built that place. The blind floor was that door, Rampo Street, they had gambling and restaurant, they built a nice place. And on the second floor was the ballroom dance hall. And the roof garden was still running, and the astroly was still running. We had competition, but he made it. I stayed with that band until Rebair and his brother fell out, and Rebair went back to working in the field, it was for white people. And Emma was in that band all that time. When I went on the boat, that's what I had to. No, I leave Rebair, and when I went to work, I did the dance with Lee Collin. And then when we leave that job, and Beans had a couple of the astroly people, and took over the astroly, not the restaurant part, but the pool table and gambling part, and upstairs. And we had about, I think it was five or six pieces. We had trumpet, sax, double uncrowned it, and David Jones on tenor. And we had four rhythms, seven. And we had the ballyhoo for them. And they'll come Sidney Desby, and he's had trouble with his badge of parade. He come to Alper with me to take the job, and I turned it down. He asked me three times. The third time I took it, because I wanted to see the guy and talk to him. In other words, I'm a guy I don't like to take that from nobody. He said, damn, I can't even remember that name. And another fellow, Don Alper, he had gave me some money, a deposit to build up his band, but I turned him down and gave him his money back. Because I knew the Streck-Food Steemboard people knew that was a good job, you see. And so I left, I leave, after we had made this recording, Randy Hall took the job. He's a very good band to play. He's like me. He studied violin. And he got to be a professor. He's out in California somewhere. He's a very good band. And went on the boat with Sidney Desvene. After work with Sidney Desvene, I worked with the Redford Band and went with the Pudon Band. I was working with the Pudon Band here. He used to play at the Country Club and all the rich white people and everything. Some blacks had a club, you know, or a Sempernore. Used to play there and a couple other places. He used to play up on Lusin Avenue, Virginia Airport, and decided to begin to lot up there. Some white men had decided to have dancing up there. You know what, there was something to do, you know, or things were slow.
Let me turn this.
I have enough space to quote you word for word. Which boat did you play on? Which of the struck was?

Well, the person I played was Fred Marwell. That was the capital. It was the wooden boat. The capital. Oh, yeah. And they had another boat called Deluxe. I believe it would come down in the summertime. And then after sitting there, they let me go and I went with the Piedhorn band. That was two boats. And Piedhorn had Walter Piedhorn playing piano, and Walter Piedhorn was such a versatile and talented man, so the captain told him, next season you could get your band together and say, we're going to have your band. There was three boats running on the river. And that was the fort around 48. We'd tramp all the way to St. Paul, tramping around them people. And then of course those things were already booked at eight at times, you see.
These were the excursion boats, not the Password? The excursion boats, yeah. Not the Password.

Yeah, excursion boats. Somewhere when I got here in 48, they dropped us off in St. Louis and I was supposed to come back. But Piedhorn went with the band out there and the captain got discouraged. I forgot to repeat that. They had Peter Bocard. And there was a lot of dissension in the band. Peter Bocard was the leader and the Tramble Brothers was supposed to be the manager and they both came over the river and there was a lot of dissension. I could see and feel it. So when I went to Chicago, like I said, the thing was going up and up so much around there and everything. And this buddy I was there, I didn't have much expense, you know. He had a small room for myself and I had wanted to go to Chicago a long time. So the rest of my house stayed there that length of time, see. And the good thing I did, because when the boat came back here, they stopped it all. The war was coming on. They stopped it all right. I was saying I wouldn't allow the fuel. You never did go back to it no more.
What was it like playing on the boats? I mean, from what I heard, you know, I heard like one thing there were a lot of fights on the boats.

At times there were. Yeah, that would be a, you see what happened, not much here. But those, St. Louis I know, a lot of those people up there, St. Louis you have what you call those, what's it called, the Irish, because they had two boats. One was a cheap boat and one was a high. They didn't have much on the boats that we were going on. They had another boat there, I can't think of it, in the Ammoor. They would fight among themselves. And they had one night, they had for color. They requested that the Catholic, but they had a lot of fun out there, the second, a few more people were Catholic. And yeah, it was St. Paul, that's what it was, I believe. But not so much on the first class boat, because if the fights they had to play, you know, those kind of people couldn't afford that. That's what I'm talking about, you see. And once in a while they had them on air, not too much air, but they always had enough sufficient support to break that up, you see. Break that up. But when we'd be a tramp, I call it tramp, down the river, you play in those different town, they'd have different group of fights, you know, but they'd get that straight in the
house.

They'd change that out, but they had enough help, or they had enough guys, but if there wasn't police, then most of the time they'd have to hire police in each city you go in, to be on the boat. I see. I see how they did that, you see. And they had a little small, and they had two smalls, you know, put them in. Sometimes they'd just line them up somewhere and put them somewhere until the boat would come back off its trip, moonlight trip, or something like that. Yeah. It's not a little while. Okay. That's where we lived there, in the other place? Versace. Versace. Versace. Versace, I know, yeah. Now, where were we at? We were talking about the steamboats. The steamboats. The excursion boats. Yeah, the excursion boats, yeah. So, yeah, I did see a way. So, I think, yeah, the part where Puron didn't go in 48, we had worked at a place on Bourbon Street there, and I think it was, oh, let's see, one, two, three, four, one, three, four blocks from, three or four blocks from Canal Street. And we got that job doing the holidays. And the man took a ride in the Puron, and he had a lady doing a partner slip thing, beautiful lady. And we were told to keep very good manners and everything. And it lasted until, yeah, you know, we played a little over the holidays. But we went through three nights. And when time the boat comes, people only didn't want to go. Captain Aldrich, and we were working at the New Orleans Country Club here on Sunday. Thought we might have been Friday and Saturday on Sunday. So, he called us out, drawn to the boat. Peter on board Peter Bookerage. And he really scoved Peter on out. I knew where it was going. I don't know if the other of them were going to drop. So, Peter on stayed on the job and took it to small pieces, about three or four pieces to work. And he said, well, it was something that helped. That's what he said. Yeah. Well, that's what it was, yeah. Because if you don't suffer with that thing that people can't hear, right? Ashton or something like that, they get up in that part of the country, it's better for them. Oh, yeah. It could be something like asthma. It's up close to asthma or something like that. I've seen them. It's something come from the trees that are in front of the flowers. Oh, yeah. Pollen or something, they call it, yeah. And when you get up in that area, it didn't have that. And here a few of you had something that didn't happen. So, that was his excuse, you see. So, that's how Peter Bookerage got in the band, because I'm repeating myself, you see. And then, like I told you, after when we got through September, I knew I could see the band wasn't going to last long. And we had a really good band. Well, you had to be good to be on the stretcher's team. Yeah. There wasn't a hire. I mean, if they did, but hire, they let you go. So, when you work that whole season, and work the next year and things, you had to be good. Then you had to have a special orshery. You go in the boat and let the captain listen at the band before he signed the contract to hire you. And I worked with Faith Marver. That was $35 the most money I ever made in my life. That was a lot of money in those days. Well, they did drop it down, the pressure dropped it down to $25, I believe. Which still wasn't too bad, because you had nothing to do. The only thing you had to pay for was to keep your clothes washed. You could wash your own clothes if you want, or whatever someone did. But they had to sit and stop, they'd tell you, well, it's going to be a laundry. For instance, they'd get in the place where they're going to pray, and two days or three days, they'll tell you. The laundry will be there. There's money coming, and pick your laundry, and bring it back the same day. And you could do some of your own washing if you want.
How was living on a boat?

One of the most wonderful things in the first getting experience. You had your tree meals a day. It's up to you if you didn't eat them. You had to miss them. That might be for her. Yeah, you know, they come out every day, and I don't have to ask them for something. I mean, I got too many friends on the boat, so I haven't moved to the public, man. I don't know if you guys would tell me, say whatever.
I was asking you how it was living on a boat.

Yeah, well, I said about three meals a day, and how you could get your clothes clean, or wash them, and do your own washing as a warmer. And at a certain time, you'd have to get new songs on, you'd have to rehearse, but we had the private, the magician had the best break on the job. Nobody would work on the evening, the captain on the down. But that was when anybody worked on the boat, it's when you get up in the morning until time to go to sleep. Everybody had something to do. And they would pick up black and whites, like guys, poor or waiters, deckhands and things like that. Someone would get, you know, get mad, or somebody would have to fire to get in trouble. And we stayed on the top deck, where all the, in other words, we considered this office, where we eat, which was considered like office. The white and the black, helpers or workers on that, they had to have them separated, but they had to set another table. The captain and his, like the ladies that worked, you see, they had a lot of little machines and things on there, operating the machines and things, root beer, things like that. They had about two white, three white ladies, and they had a colored lady and a colored gentleman. They'd been waiting for them a long time. But we'd sleep on the top. In other words, you were just like an official or something. But the other part of the white and the black, some slept on the dance floor and the deckhands slept down in the hall. Now, one black guy, they were waiting for them for a long time. He was dressed up as lightning, the captain, had a uniform and everything. But you see, sometime that boat would have to land somewhere, and it wasn't the proper place. I'd see them land, they'd find this guy out there with a little bit of rope, he'd swim. And he'd get to that tree or railroad track, and I'd say, how the hell did they put that thing on a railroad track? It's dangerous, you know? But they knew what they were doing. And he'd get that little rope, and then he'd put that big rope in. And they'd send the railroad back, and it'd be a difficult place to land, you see. You had to have a man like that. A lot of times, something would go wrong. They'd have to stop in some place and have something done. They had one place. They had a, oh, it was like a big tank, I would say. I can't think of the town. All ships that run on the river could go there and dock up and get a quick repair or a long repair. But we'd always try to get a quick repair, because the captain wouldn't let his boat go that bad, that far, you see. I can't think of that place. We played that city. And it had the river block off like a, you know, this is a bit like a big tank. Must have been about two blocks, three blocks wide, or about eight, six, eight blocks long. And at that time Uncle Sam was building locks on the river, so they'd hold the water back. And that's how they started putting these excursion boats on us. Try like my truck, you try with one, you went with two, and you went with three. Because once in a while we'd get stuck on a sandbar. And that meant you had to play there until they'd get off that sandbar. You'd get stuck on a sandbar in the moonlight. You got to stay there until they'd get off that sandbar.
What's the longest you got stuck on a sandbar?

Oh, I mean, well, they had to figure out that thing to work with. I mean, I remember, because I mean, we'd be praying, and we'd get tired, you know what I mean? You get tired, but you got to pray. Be getting people happy. And I remember sometime, before the war, you remember, I know you wouldn't remember about that, during the robbery, you probably would, but before, I'm going to say I went into the war, and I went into the war, there were people committing suicide. That was, we would jump off that bull.
Remember that?

Yeah. But it was a happy thing, and people would enjoy themselves. Now, there was women, men would sneak alcohol on us. They sold root beer. They didn't sell no alcohol, but they sold beer, I think. They sold beer. I know strong, but women would sneak as ever. Men would sneak their bottles. We did the same thing. We'd sneak our bottles. But don't let them catch you drunk. Don't let them get the musician on that stand drunk while he can't do his job. And then there was help. From the deckhand to the porter and the cashiers and everything. Don't mess with them. I mean, you had to be on the lake. And this man, this black man, and this woman, I know they weren't in the race or nothing, but, and this other black guy I told you about, that was his daddy, my son, I got to believe his daddy. He was the head man for the deckhand. He controlled them. Sometimes they had white deckhand, they didn't want to listen to him, but he'd go. He'd let them all. But that man had experience, he knew what to do. And I say a captain has a whole lot of responsibility on his end, but he had a lot of assistance. He'd always have about six guys, white guys, and one black guy worked for him a long time. He did everything. And he could trust them, he knew them. He had one guy got killed in Davenport. He'd be waiting for the cup of the slalom, nobody would look and see how it happened. But he went out that Saturday night and got drunk. And they had two of them, a sternum on each side. Not a sternum, but the thing that pushed his sternum back there. And he went to come in and get soap off as possible, and this thing had stopped. And before this engineer does that, he rings the bell. He didn't hear that bell. He had this thing down in there. Before we get to this thing that's going this way, it's one thing going this way, then it's very very good thing going this way.
And he had his head down in there and the man pushed that button.

And nobody can understand, because that man has been working with him for so many years. So yeah, I actually think it can happen if the person knows the danger of certain things. You see? And another guy, he's from Spain, and he and I used to talk a lot, because he always had a little fishing place. You could fish if you want. He loved eel. He and I used to talk, that's in a time when Spain was having trouble among the government. Well, I used to talk to him about the situation, how that happened. And that's why he left Spain, because I think it was a comic or something that was trying to take over Spain, which they did in a while, I think. This is about in the 30s, them talking about. They had a big war.
Before the war.
Before the war.
Oh, before the war.
Yeah, they had a big war. That's when a little general or something got in there. A small fella. Yeah. He took over the emperor, the king of Spain, was it?
Yeah. Dictator.
Dictator. He was a dictator. Yeah. He was on the communist side. Well, you know he did it pretty well.
No. No, he was on the German side. He was not a fascist. Oh, fascist.
That's what I was. Well, I skipped about one point. Yeah, fascist. That's right. You're right.
That's right.

You know, you had time to do it. Yeah. Oh. So, like I said, when we get to Tower, where we're going to be in two days? You know, I think most of two days. It'll be a Saturday, a Sunday, a big stop time. Well, everybody had a chance to go out and have a little fun. And then sometimes if it's a one-stop time and it's not leaving at night, you're leaving that morning. But you can't even know what you're going to want. You want to have some fun, sex, anything you wanted to do. You see? You know, he knew that. But don't miss that boat, man. Don't miss that boat.
You know, there's a couple of guys that did it.

And they were lucky that he'd accept them back. Well, there must have been some guys that he probably needed, he couldn't get. Because it was always, like I said, ordinary, simple job, like cleaning up like that, white or black, they'd hide. But they always kept their main crew as people that they could trust. You see? And they always had any man who was black or this white that could do the job that he was supervising and had a choice to tell the guys the guys were to do. The white and the black. And this man, this black woman, they slept on the top deck. She was like a maid. And he was like a, he did most everything. Because they had food on there. That one black man they pick up somewhere for food. And this other black fellow, he raised his farm level and he did most anything he could do. And it was like this guy would work on the deck and wore the uniform suit. And when I first started with that, you just knew what to do. And everybody would go out when they knew the town, you know. Have a little fun, I'll put it that way. You speak to the guys, like, they're working for the people. They're wise in New York, you see. And when you go into town like that, people just looking for you. It's like with the circus, I don't know if you know anything about that. The circus is a part of us who would come into town, everybody's looking for the suckers. You see. So you're well trained to know how to protect yourself.
You know, those were some happy days, man. So living and working on a boat, you were living pretty high then?

Oh boy, yeah, yeah. I don't know, I don't know. Good food, good? Good food, you had your food every day. And the captain would tell you, he said, look, when you tell you got two guys, some stubborn heads, he said, look here, I noticed here when we first started, he said, you, you're going to pick up a whole lot of weight since you've been eating three meals a day and resting a lot. He doesn't tell me that I do that. And I was very, I knew he was tricky, I was always, didn't want to. One time, he caught me. I went out, I said, my hair got bad. And he called me in this office. I said, what you going to do? If you did something wrong with somebody and you manage it or your superior attorney or
you acknowledge it.

So I begged pardon to him, I said, sorry, I did wrong, Captain. And I was really a drunk man. Yeah, I can see my life, I've, well, I'll put it this way, I've been, God bless. I've been in some dangerous situations and bad places and things. Sevolga, traveling on the boat. In fact, we go on concert tours and different things like that.
Do you do much traveling now?

Yeah, we have some. We were, well, we were, well, we were, well, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, we were, You heard what I said about my travel thing I did. Before, 24, I went to Chicago, I was waiting for this track for the steamboat line, and then there's a preservation hall. I know what they expected, and how they carry them, I shall. Now this is a place where I have large work companies, even north of South Dakota went out in that area, with the chalky music bars. And we were, in fact, everywhere we went was sensation, because we knew how to carry ourselves. And there's an Indian reservation out there. Just for curiosity, we went to a truck and then sneaked up some whiskey, but we weren't supposed to have it. And we had some white people who invited us to a place, and some were resented, but it wasn't their business. We all knew how to carry ourselves.
Mm-hmm.

You see? And some places I played up north, had more hatred for the black man than they have in the South. Yeah, and out of the cold, that's right, I want to get you that. It's the sugar beet. Mm-hmm. There was a man with a truck would go pick these people somewhere. I don't know if they went all the way to Mexico, but they were from up in that area. Because a black person probably would do it. It's too down there because they had to be doing this all day long. Oh, yeah. And the Asian, Japanese, Chinese, they could do that, and then South America, some Mexican, they could do that. Excuse me. And we happened to be at the time. I used to go out there and watch and look at them. I'd talk, because I'm talking to the U.S. by now, you see. We found a place for them. They weren't accepted, because it was likely to not accept it up here. But if they need the money, we'd go all over to Mexico to get them, bring them back, and pay them a fairly good price, not the price we'd pay American. No, I had that wrong. Some of them, they did a lot of cheating and everything. But they said we pay them a fair price, and they would go all fine. You could see them with their families and everything, you know, out of the Spanish and things like that. And we happened to be with them at the time. I used to go look at them. And I said, I said, hell, I couldn't do that myself. And I ran her by the Asiatic, the Spanish, some of them were in the South America mixed up with Africa. And the Asian people there, and the Indian, whatever we call our Indian year, and the Spanish. And the Italian do it. I mean, they come up with it, you know. That was another experience.

How do you feel now, I mean, you know, like in the last few years, you've been getting a lot more recognition for your playing than you used to? You know, like, you know, one thing is, you know, like the Novak tape. I suppose going on tour with the Jaffees. I mean, how do you feel about, you know, just...

I feel very grateful and thankful for it, because what you're saying, as a subject, if it wasn't for that police officer enough, we wouldn't have had that opportunity to do that. The preservation people are doing it for us. Other guys, a higher class, like when they had the big band that was popular, they did it. Which I did in Chicago, I told you about that. But most of these guys didn't have that opportunity. And I am thankful for it. I was speaking for myself, for the President of the Hartwell, they did in the US, bringing us to these different places. I told you about the Fools we had in Russia.
No, I haven't heard that much about it. That was true.
Our government and the Russian government, I can tell you about that.
That was with Kid Thomas?

Yeah, I don't know how they selected this band. That's their business. Yeah. You see? And we were really treated very wonderfully. How was the response to... That's what I said, the response. They had three fans in there. They have a jazz, one city up in the government, and they have a jazz club, which I was very much surprised. In Russia? Because every place I went before that, they have them. Yeah. And I got some recordure they gave us. They copied the big bands back there when they were popular in the 30s, the farthest black and white, and they copied us everywhere I went, but I was surprised. And they had what we call a jam session. We do that, the manas jam, they mix that around. And they had, it looked like it was a small theater. They had three different bands I could see. But the proper one was six, some was seven, some was eight. And the trouble there with the banjos, it's hard for them to get good banjos. The only way they can get it closer is through East Berlin. So I told them, I said, in West Berlin, I know there's a bigger company kind of company, because Kim Warren, his band, he bought from there. It's a very good banjo. But the other instruments are pretty good, very good. And those guys can play. They can play, yeah.
And they play jazz in Russian?

I'm telling you, when I'm talking to some of you they're playing just like us. They're playing Sedition and some of them are playing Dixieland. And they have the all-in-folk songs. Like when you're in the hotel you stay and you go in the dining room where they have, you know, bands just like that. They use their folk songs and some of them switch around to, like I tell you, I did my time, but different types of music. You see? And they're very ordinary. Very ordinary. It's like it's supposed to be. I don't see anybody can cheat over there. I don't think. We want to revisit each city we were in. We'd be a week and we'd have one or two days. They'd be sponsored by the government for sightseeing. And besides that, Redmen and I, we'd go out ourselves and walk. We didn't know where we were. We'd use a guideline, you know, like the Indians do right there. And they're all friendly. They know you. They know where you were. They got the news from it. And they look at you and tell you you're not them. The Redmen almost looked like a Russian. A lot of people confused. They said, no.
They said, no, I'm from the state in New Orleans. And I said, no, no.

And with some place we stopped going to Russia, met a couple, men and his wife. Something like I'm talking to you. I like to talk to you if you want me to talk. Anyway, I got to talk to them and I found out that the wife was born in Russia. She speak of Russia. No, they're from St. Paul, Twin City. And they wanted to visit Russia. We were on the same plane and everything. And the plane stopped and everything. That's why I got to talk to them. And I met some Africans. I forgot what part of Africa. They were studying science, engineering, doctors and everything. But the Russian was studying. And the musicians, they were playing Dixieland and they were playing traditional music too. And we made a lot of friends. A lot of friends. And some of those places, I guess they sold a lot of tickets a lot of people wanted to go. That's why I was there a week in one place, you know, to give other people a chance to see. And when we would, the San Bernardino States, when you're in the band, a lot of time come here and it's leaving, where it's playing, everybody wants you to hurry up and sign, you know, and you ain't got time. You push the time. People would stand out there the bus in the cold, which wasn't cool for them because it was cool for us. I didn't see no sun on ice, but it was cool. They want to get to you. And I said, we have to get on the bus to get back, you see. And so what I'm subject to, the main part of the subject is that United States jazz is making history all over the world.
Yeah. And it's probably more appreciated in other places. That's what I'm talking about.
I didn't say it that way, but it's really appreciated.
Yeah.

Because the people have the fine musicians playing just like us. And they have albums or jazz that they give you that they record and you perceive for yourself and you hear them playing. You see how they are. That's what we gave to the world, United States. Especially in the already jazz. Do you know how jazz was supposed to spell? J-A-S-S. Right? They used to have an old drummer at the Hall. I don't know if it's still got it. That's where it really fell. But it got so offensive because you saw it put the Z behind it. See, here you always had a certain class of people that didn't appreciate this kind of music way back then. They called it low down. Low class of music people, white and black.
Well, it was at least a lot of people associated with the whorehouses.
